content: Delafloxacin is indicated for the treatment of acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI) caused by susceptible bacteria. The recommended dosage is 300 mg administered intravenously (IV) every 12 hours for 5 to 14 days. Alternatively, treatment can begin with 300 mg IV every 12 hours, followed by a switch to a 450-mg oral tablet every 12 hours for 5 to 14 days. Another option is 450 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 to 14 days. Delafloxacin is also indicated for the treatment of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP) caused by susceptible bacteria. The recommended dosage is 300 mg IV every 12 hours for 5 to 10 days. Alternatively, treatment can start with 300 mg IV every 12 hours, followed by a switch to a 450-mg oral tablet every 12 hours for 5 to 10 days. Another option is 450 mg orally every 12 hours for 5 to 10 days. The safety and efficacy of delafloxacin have not been established in certain populations. Both delafloxacin and fexinidazole can prolong the QTc interval, and their coadministration should be avoided. Additionally, fexinidazole should not be used with drugs that block potassium channels or prolong the QT interval. Delafloxacin may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Delafloxacin interacts with various agents that can decrease its absorption in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract due to cation binding. These agents include aluminum hydroxide, calcium acetate, calcium carbonate, calcium chloride, calcium citrate, calcium gluconate, magnesium chloride, magnesium gluconate, magnesium oxide, magnesium sulfate, magnesium supplements, manganese, multivitamins, polysaccharide iron, ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, ferrous sulfate, ferric maltol, and zinc. To minimize these interactions, oral delafloxacin should be administered at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after these agents. Therapy should be modified or closely monitored in these cases. Delafloxacin may increase the toxicity of amifampridine, which can cause seizures. Coadministration with drugs that lower the seizure threshold should be avoided. Delafloxacin may also increase the effects of warfarin, requiring close monitoring. Patients treated with selinexor may experience neurological toxicities, and coadministration with medications that cause dizziness or confusion should be avoided. Fluoroquinolones, including delafloxacin, have been associated with serious and potentially irreversible adverse reactions, such as tendinitis, tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and central nervous system (CNS) effects. If any of these reactions occur, the drug should be discontinued immediately, and systemic fluoroquinolones should be avoided in such patients. Fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness in patients with myasthenia gravis and should be avoided in those with a known history of the condition. Delafloxacin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to the drug, its components, or other fluoroquinolones. Prescribing antibiotics in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to provide benefit and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Epidemiologic studies have observed an increased risk of aortic aneurysm and dissection within two months of fluoroquinolone use, particularly in elderly patients. The etiology is unknown, and fluoroquinolones should only be used in patients at risk for aortic aneurysm when no alternative antibacterial treatments are available. Blood glucose disturbances, including symptomatic hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia, have been reported with fluoroquinolones, particularly in diabetic patients receiving concomitant treatment with oral hypoglycemic agents (e.g., glyburide) or insulin. Severe cases of hypoglycemia resulting in coma or death have been reported with other fluoroquinolones. Blood glucose levels should be carefully monitored, and therapy should be discontinued immediately if a hypoglycemic reaction occurs. Data on the use of delafloxacin in pregnant women are limited and insufficient to determine the risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. It is unknown if delafloxacin is distributed in human breast milk, but it has been excreted in the breast milk of rats. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered alongside the mother’s clinical need for the drug and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed infant. Delafloxacin should be infused intravenously over 60 minutes using a volume control set or piggyback container. The drug may be taken with or without food. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as possible within 4 hours of the missed dose. If more than 4 hours have passed, the patient should wait until the next scheduled dose. Tablets and lyophilized powder should be stored at controlled room temperature (20–25°C or 68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Reconstituted vials can be stored for up to 24 hours refrigerated (2–8°C or 36–46°F) or at controlled room temperature until further diluted for IV infusion. Diluted solutions can also be stored for up to 24 hours refrigerated or at room temperature but should not be frozen.
